Title: Elecciones 2026 en América Latina: Un Adelanto

Summary: 
Colombia is preparing for its 2026 presidential and legislative elections, with key dates set for March 8 (legislative voting and internal party primaries), May 31 (first round of presidential elections, with a potential runoff on June 21), and July 28 (presidential inauguration). The president must win over 50% of the vote in the first round to avoid a runoff; in a second round, the majority winner takes office for a non-renewable four-year term. The Senate will have 103 seats, including 100 elected via proportional representation and two reserved for indigenous communities, with the second-place presidential candidate automatically receiving a Senate seat. The Chamber of Representatives will have between 165 and 182 seats, depending on census data, including seats for Afro-Colombian, indigenous, and diaspora communities, conflict-affected regions, and an additional seat for the second-place presidential running mate. Re-election is allowed for both chambers. Voter turnout averages 46%, with 55% in the 2022 presidential first round, and voting is not mandatory, including for Colombians abroad. Despite President Gustavo Petro’s 57% disapproval rating, a weakened peace plan, and political violence, his legacy continues to influence the race. A November 2025 Invamer poll shows 81% of Colombians prioritize strong U.S. relations, benefiting right-wing candidate Abelardo de la Espriella, a Trump, Milei, and Bukele admirer, who ranked second with 18%. However, leftist appeal remains strong: 37% identify as right-wing, but nearly 25% identify as left-wing, and former senator Iván Cepeda leads with 32% support. Petro’s 38% base remains significant despite his ineligibility for re-election. With a record 107 pre-candidates, top contenders include centrist Sergio Fajardo, conservative Miguel Uribe Londoño, and progressive Claudia López. The March 8 elections will serve as a critical early indicator of momentum.

Published date: December 17 2025, 12:00

Title: La reorganización del tablero político de cara a las elecciones para la Cámara en el Atlántico

The upcoming March 8, 2026, legislative election in Atlántico Department, Colombia, is shaping up as one of the most competitive in recent history, with 78 candidates across 13 lists vying for seven seats in the Chamber of Representatives. The political landscape features a mix of established figures and emerging leaders, including influencers such as Felipe Saruma (5M+ Instagram followers) and Lily Díaz, daughter of Diomedes Díaz, both appearing on conservative and Cambio Radical lists. In the 2022 elections, seats were distributed among Cambio Radical (3), Partido Liberal (2), Pacto Histórico (1), and Partido Conservador (1). This cycle, incumbents Gersel Pérez, Agmeth Escaf, and Armando Zabaraín are seeking Senate seats, while Dolcey Torres, Modesto Aguilera, and Betsy Pérez are not running, leaving Jezmi Barraza as the sole Liberal candidate seeking re-election. Experts Alejandro Blanco Zúñiga and Juan Fernando Gutiérrez project Cambio Radical and the Liberal Party as the strongest forces, each likely securing two seats. Samir Radi, Estefanel Gutiérrez, and Welfran Mendoza are seen as key contenders from Cambio Radical. The Pacto Histórico is expected to retain one seat, likely going to Jaime Santamaría. The Center Democratic coalition (Nuevo Liberalismo, Mira) is backed by Álvaro Uribe and Senator Carlos Meisel, with Juan Restrepo as their candidate, seen as a strong contender due to national polarization. The Partido Conservador is projected to win one seat with Juan Camilo Fuentes. A potential eighth seat could go to Wisner Sandoval (Demócrata) via the Afro-descendant constituency, supported by former Senator Eduardo Pulgar. Laureano Acuña of the Partido de La U aims to surprise by returning to Congress, emphasizing authenticity, permanence, and focus on rural areas. Samir Radi highlights energy affordability, youth employment, and economic growth as central goals. Juan Carlos Restrepo emphasizes economic development, productive education, and social security, while Estefanel Gutiérrez calls for transformation in municipalities, citing Barranquilla’s model as a blueprint. The absence of additional seats created by the peace agreement means the race is now more tightly contested, with national polarization expected to heavily influence outcomes.

The Uribismo political movement in Florida has activated its electoral machinery, warning that low diaspora voter turnout could allow a candidate similar to President Gustavo Petro to win a seat in Colombia's Chamber of Representatives. Jaime Flórez, a journalist and activist, issued a stark warning, stating that despite massive Venezuelan protests, Colombia elected a former guerrilla leader, and now a similar profile leads in polls—calling the upcoming March election a plebiscite on democracy. Recent polls show Senator Iván Cepeda, a key ally of President Petro, slightly ahead, prompting alarm in opposition ranks. Economic pragmatism was emphasized by Murcia, who highlighted remittances—equivalent to 33% of Colombia’s exports—as a vital economic pillar and called for eliminating bureaucratic barriers to property ownership and access to virtual SENA education. He also proposed transforming the inefficient consular service into a robust support network. Fabio Andrade, party director in the U.S., invoked memories of exile and warned against repeating the fates of Venezuela and Cuba, urging immediate jurado de votación registration for transparency. Olga Lucía Murcia and Camilo Florido stressed party unity, with Murcia linking diaspora struggles to support for the Uribe-led Senate list and Paloma Valencia’s presidential bid, while Florido defended the Centro Democrático as the institutional pivot preventing democratic collapse since 2013. The political climate is highly polarized, with opposition seeking to capitalize on public discontent over security and economy after four years of Colombia’s first left-wing government. The March 8 election will determine Congress composition and serve as a critical real-world poll ahead of the 2026 presidential first round. For Uribismo, regaining the international seat and expanding its legislative base is essential for political control from 2026 to 2030.

Title: Reacomodo en la derecha paisa: quiénes se bajan y cuáles llegan a la Cámara

Summary: 
In the lead-up to the 2026 legislative elections in Antioquia, Colombia, significant political reshuffling is underway, particularly on the right-wing spectrum. Of the 18 current representatives from Antioquia, at least half are expected to leave the Chamber of Representatives—either to run for the Senate, prepare for the 2027 local elections, or pursue other professional paths. The Centro Democrático is renewing its slate: three current representatives—Jhon Jairo Berrío, Óscar Darío Pérez, and Yulieth Sánchez—seek re-election, while Hernán Cadavid and Juan Espinal aim for Senate seats. Espinal’s candidacy hinges on Paola Holguín’s continued presidential candidacy, which remains uncertain until March. If Holguín drops out, she may run for Governor of Antioquia, and Espinal would succeed her in the Senate, with Juan Sebastián Abad replacing him in the Chamber. Andrés Guerra, former presidential candidate, has stepped down from the Senate race and will instead lead the Chamber list, a move he accepted reluctantly despite having received 67,761 votes in 2022. The movement led by Medellín’s Mayor Federico Gutiérrez, Creemos, is also entering the race with Luis Guillermo Patiño—former Education Secretary of Medellín—heading the Chamber list, backed by Andrés Bedoya. Other contenders include Germán Darío Hoyos, Simón Molina, Juliana Gutiérrez (the mayor’s sister), and José Miguel Zuluaga. The Conservative Party, currently holding three Chamber seats, faces major changes: only Luis Miguel López will retain his current political backing; Andrés Felipe Jiménez, having split from Juan Diego Gómez, will run independently with Juan Carlos Wills; Daniel Restrepo will run for Senate, and Jaime Cano, previously removed for dual militancy, seeks a Chamber seat. Germán Blanco, from the 'Consenso' faction, will seek re-election and back Juan Camilo Callejas, also previously removed for dual militancy. Creemos aims for at least three Chamber seats, with political momentum built from Gutiérrez’s strong regional performance in the 2023 local elections.

Fabio Andrade, party director in the U.S., invoked memories of exile and warned against repeating the fates of Venezuela and Cuba, urging immediate jurado de votación registration for transparency. Olga Lucía Murcia and Camilo Florido stressed party unity, with Murcia linking diaspora struggles to support for the Uribe-led Senate list and Paloma Valencia’s presidential bid, while Florido defended the Centro Democrático as the institutional pivot preventing democratic collapse since 2013. The political climate is highly polarized, with opposition seeking to capitalize on public discontent over security and economy after four years of Colombia’s first left-wing government. The March 8 election will determine Congress composition and serve as a critical real-world poll ahead of the 2026 presidential first round. For Uribismo, regaining the international seat and expanding its legislative base is essential for political control from 2026 to 2030.

articles.title: Colombia’s Peace Curule Elections 2026: Seven Incumbents Seek Re-election Amid Scrutiny and Challenges
articles.summary: The Colombian Registraduría Nacional del Estado Civil has released the final list of candidates for the 2026 legislative elections in the Circunscripciones Transitorias Especiales de Paz (CITREP), which are reserved seats in the Chamber of Representatives for victims of the armed conflict. Seven of the 16 current peace curule representatives have announced their intention to seek re-election. A total of 122 lists with 246 candidates are competing for these seats, which are set to expire after the 2026–2030 legislative term, as established by the 2016 Peace Accord. The candidates must be victims of the conflict, reside in or have been displaced from the designated territories, and cannot have recent ties to traditional political parties. Each list must include one man and one woman running independently. Notable candidates include Karen Astrid Manrique Olarte, who faces corruption allegations linked to the Unidad Nacional para la Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (UNGRD), and Jorge Rodrigo Tovar Vélez, son of 'Jorge 40', a former AUC paramilitary commander. Despite the mechanism’s intent to ensure inclusion, past challenges included threats, violence, and financial barriers due to strict funding requirements. The 2026 election will be the final opportunity for these communities to have parliamentary representation. The UNGRD, responsible for disaster risk management, has come under scrutiny for corruption allegations, underscoring the need for transparency in state institutions, particularly in post-conflict regions where trust is critical.

articles.title: Candidates for Colombia's Chamber of Representatives from Santander Debate in First Forum
articles.summary: On Thursday, February 19, 2026, ten candidates leading their respective lists for the Colombian Chamber of Representatives will participate in a live debate organized by the Comité Intergremial de Santander. The event, broadcast from 5:00 PM via social media platforms of Vanguardia, Universidad Autónoma de Bucaramanga (Unab), Metropolitano, and Canal TRO, features candidates Sergio Arenas (Centro Democrático), Luis Roberto Ordóñez (Liga de Gobernantes Anticorrupción), Mario José Carvajal (Partido Liberal), Camilo Torres (Pacto Histórico), Aleida Noguera (Coalición Avanza), Roberto Ávila (Nuevo Liberalismo), Jairo Cala (Fuerza Ciudadana), Ferley Sierra (Alianza Verde), Juan Carlos Celis (Cambio Radical), Lina Barrera (Partido Conservador), and Sergio Isnardo Muñoz (Partido de la 'U'). The debate aims to present their policy proposals ahead of the congressional elections, in which over 80 candidates are vying for seven seats allocated to the Santander department. The event also includes participation from ANDI, Prosantander, Cotelco, Camacol, the Instituto de Estudios Políticos de la Unab, Bucaramanga Metropolitana Cómo Vamos, and Fenavi.

articles.title: Major Parties in Colombia Finalize Senate Top Candidates Ahead of 2026 Elections
articles.summary: With the deadline for 2026 congressional candidate registrations approaching, major political parties in Colombia have finalized their top candidates for the Senate. The Pacto Histórico, seeking to continue the leftist agenda of President Gustavo Petro, retained Carolina Corcho, former Minister of Health, as its Senate head. In 2022, the coalition won 20 Senate seats with 2.8 million votes. The main opposition party, Centro Democrático, led by former President Álvaro Uribe, selected Andrés Forero, a current representative, as its Senate candidate; in 2022, it secured 13 seats with 1.9 million votes. Cambio Radical, led by former Vice President Germán Vargas Lleras, chose Senator Carlos Fernando Motoa, who previously helped the party win 11 seats and 1.6 million votes. The Liberal Party, led by former President César Gaviria, named current Congress President Lidio García as its Senate head; the party obtained 14 seats and 2.1 million votes in 2022. The Conservative Party selected David Barguil, which earned 15 seats and 2.2 million votes in the previous election. The Partido de La U, divided internally between Petro supporters and opposition, chose Juan Felipe Lemus as its Senate candidate, having won 10 seats and 1.5 million votes in 2022. Other parties also announced their leads: Alianza Verde selected Luis Eduardo Garzón, Salvación Nacional chose Enrique Gómez, and the coalition Ahora Colombia (Dignidad, Mira, Nuevo Liberalismo) selected current representative Juan Sebastián Gómez.

articles.title: Political Parties Intensify Candidate List Adjustments Ahead of 2026 Colombian Legislative Elections
articles.summary: Numerous political movements are underway across Colombian parties to finalize their legislative candidate lists ahead of the 2026 elections. Key deadlines require submissions to the Registraduría by December 8, 2025. The Centro Democrático has intensified its efforts, with former President Álvaro Uribe Vélez playing a decisive role. Hernán Cadavid and Andrés Forero are moving from the Chamber to the Senate, while Daniel Briceño is transitioning from the Bogotá City Council to the Chamber, following Uribe’s endorsement due to his political oversight and criticism of President Gustavo Petro’s government. Eduard Triana will replace Ciro Ramírez in the Senate from Boyacá, and Andrés Guerra will lead the Uribista list in Antioquia after Cadavid’s move. These two regions are critical for the party’s electoral base. In Alianza Verde, recent party meetings have led to candidates like Katherine Miranda, Cristian Avendaño, and Olga Lucía Velásquez aiming for the Senate in 2026. This shift has changed the lead candidates in Bogotá (Catherine Juvinao), Santander, and Cundinamarca (Gloria Liliana Ramírez, who will also be Velásquez’s running mate). The Liberal Party is also experiencing major changes, with nearly 10 of its 37 Chamber representatives seeking Senate seats, including Juan Carlos Losada, Leonardo Gallego, Álvaro Monedero, Héctor Chaparro, María Eugenia Lopera, and Oscar Hernán Sánchez, with Gaviria’s approval for the latter two. The Conservative Party is similarly seeing internal shifts, with Wadith Manzur (Córdoba) seeking a Senate seat despite ongoing corruption investigations, alongside Juan Carlos Wills and Luis Eduardo Díaz Mateus, who have party backing to advance their campaigns.

articles.title: Political Reconfiguration on Antioquia’s Right: Who’s Leaving and Who’s Coming to the Chamber
articles.summary: In the lead-up to the 2026 legislative elections in Antioquia, Colombia, significant political reshuffling is underway, particularly on the right-wing spectrum. Of the 18 current representatives from Antioquia, at least half are expected to leave the Chamber of Representatives—either to run for the Senate, prepare for the 2027 local elections, or pursue other professional paths. The Centro Democrático is renewing its slate: three current representatives—Jhon Jairo Berrío, Óscar Darío Pérez, and Yulieth Sánchez—seek re-election, while Hernán Cadavid and Juan Espinal aim for Senate seats. Espinal’s candidacy hinges on Paola Holguín’s continued presidential candidacy, which remains uncertain until March. If Holguín drops out, she may run for Governor of Antioquia, and Espinal would succeed her in the Senate, with Juan Sebastián Abad replacing him in the Chamber. Andrés Guerra, former presidential candidate, has stepped down from the Senate race and will instead lead the Chamber list, a move he accepted reluctantly despite having received 67,761 votes in 2022. The movement led by Medellín’s Mayor Federico Gutiérrez, Creemos, is also entering the race with Luis Guillermo Patiño—former Education Secretary of Medellín—heading the Chamber list, backed by Andrés Bedoya. Other contenders include Germán Darío Hoyos, Simón Molina, Juliana Gutiérrez (the mayor’s sister), and José Miguel Zuluaga. The Conservative Party, currently holding three Chamber seats, faces major changes: only Luis Miguel López will retain his current political backing; Andrés Felipe Jiménez, having split from Juan Diego Gómez, will run independently with Juan Carlos Wills; Daniel Restrepo will run for Senate, and Jaime Cano, previously removed for dual militancy, seeks a Chamber seat. Germán Blanco, from the 'Consenso' faction, will seek re-election and back Juan Camilo Callejas, also previously removed for dual militancy. Creemos aims for at least three Chamber seats, with political momentum built from Gutiérrez’s strong regional performance in the 2023 local elections.
